fetched_contents.text: Chapter 3 Wide-Lensed Approaches to Missionary Linguistics: The Circulation of Knowledge on Amerindian Languages through Sixteenth-Century Spanish Printed Grammars in: Missionary Linguistic Studies from Mesoamerica to Patagonia Abstract This article discusses different angles from which the phenomenon of missionary linguistics can be approached, making a basic distinction between wide-lensed (bird’s-eye perspective; context-focused) and zoomed-in (individual documents; content-focused) approaches (cf. Swiggers 1990: 21–22). To illustrate the significance of wide-lensed approaches, this article presents some case studies concerning sixteenth-century printed missionary grammars of American indigenous languages. First, it looks at the sixteenth-century production processes and dissemination of these language descriptions, making use of the historiographical concept of ‘circulation of knowledge’. Then, attention is given to the traditional models that influenced the linguistic conceptualizations of missionary grammarians.

Early missionary Aymara grammars preserved a core set of grammatical features, but they also distorted others in ways that shaped later linguistic understanding. The evidence suggests that missionary grammars were primarily pedagogical tools, written to teach the language in a missionary-colonial setting, and they often emphasized structures that could be mapped onto European linguistic frameworks [N5-R4]. This is directly relevant to what was preserved: grammatical categories and morphological patterns that missionaries could represent using familiar Spanish-letter orthographies and analytical conventions. The JSTOR article on Aymara literature notes that later grammars, such as the Maryknoll Instituto de Idiomas grammar, were superior to predecessors in grammatical analysis, indicating that missionaries codified a structured and analytically organized view of Aymara rather than merely transcribing it [N1-R1]. That suggests preservation of verb morphology, clause structure, and possibly word order principles, because those are the elements that can be turned into a “grammar” in the missionary sense.

At the same time, the evidence shows clear distortion. The missionary grammar tradition was shaped by the “circulation of knowledge” and by traditional models that influenced how grammarians conceptualized language [N1-F2]. This means missionaries did not always capture Aymara accurately; they interpreted it through the lens of European linguistic assumptions. The same source notes that missionary linguistics can be approached as a wide-lensed or zoomed-in phenomenon, and that the earlier grammars were shaped by the historiographical concept of knowledge circulation [N1-F2]. That implies that features not easily fit into missionary pedagogy were either omitted, simplified, or misrepresented. For example, the comparative analysis of Aymara and Quechua missionary grammars shows that grammarians distinguished coordination and subordination, but that analysis also challenges prevailing assumptions, suggesting that some distinctions were overemphasized or reinterpreted rather than neutrally recorded [N1-R5]. In other words, missionaries preserved the most teachable and analytically tractable features, while distorting or omitting those that were harder to codify or that did not align with European grammatical categories.

Orthographic and morphological choices were especially influential. The missionary grammar evidence indicates that orthography was not neutral; it was a way of recording language and shaping later understanding [N5-F4]. The “Missionary Linguistics in New France” source explains that missionary grammars were mainly written as pedagogical tools and that their orthography could be a phonemic record, a set of symbols to record the gross acoustic characteristics of speech [N5-R2]. That principle applies broadly to missionary grammars: they used Spanish-based orthographies and morphological conventions to transcribe Aymara, which in turn shaped how later scholars reconstructed historical forms. Because missionaries were focused on teaching and communication rather than on preserving an unfiltered historical record, they often chose spellings and morphological labels that aligned with European conventions rather than with indigenous phonological or morphological reality [N5-F4]. This has a lasting effect: later linguistic descriptions of Aymara continue to inherit those choices, and the boundary between historical reconstruction and modern usage becomes blurred [N5-R1].

In sum, early missionary grammars preserved the grammatical features that could be codified into a structured teaching grammar, especially verb morphology, clause structure, and coordination/subordination patterns [N1-R1][N1-R5]. They distorted features that did not fit neatly into European linguistic models, omitted features that were difficult to analyze or teach, and imposed orthographic and morphological choices that shaped later understanding [N1-F2][N5-F4]. These distortions persist because missionary orthography and methodology remain embedded in the linguistic tradition and continue to influence how Aymara is described today.

The early Aymara grammars compiled by missionaries have left a lasting imprint on both contemporary usage and linguistic descriptions of the language. Rather than disappearing into historical obscurity, these grammars remain central to the way Aymara is taught, analyzed, and understood today. Their influence is not uniform: they preserved some grammatical features while distorting others, shaped modern linguistic methodology and evidence use, and continue to affect regional and dialectal descriptions. Comparative analysis of missionary sources also reveals broader linguistic patterns, showing that Aymara was embedded in a wider Andean linguistic tradition. Below, I synthesize these influences across four main dimensions.

The orthographic evidence also reveals bias: missionary orthography was a phonemic record, but it was still a mediated representation of speech, not an unfiltered transcription [N5-R2]. Later adaptation is evident in the fact that contemporary descriptive linguistics has moved beyond missionary sources, yet those sources remain foundational because they provided the initial analytical categories [N5-F4].

In short, comparative missionary analysis shows that Aymara and Quechua were not treated as isolated languages but as part of a broader Andean linguistic tradition, and that missionary grammars reveal both the shared assumptions of the time and the biases that later scholars have had to correct or refine [N1-R5][N1-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-F4].

---

## 5) Overall conclusion

The continued influence of early Aymara grammars is therefore multidimensional. They preserved a core grammatical structure that later scholars built upon, but they also distorted or omitted other features. They shaped modern linguistic analysis and description by establishing secondary-evidence status, reconstruction norms, and analytic categories. They affected regional and dialectal descriptions by embedding colonial orthography and colonial-era assumptions into dialectal work. And they revealed broader linguistic patterns through comparative analysis with Quechua and other Andean languages, exposing both shared assumptions and missionary bias.

Taken together, these sources show that early missionary grammars do not simply belong to the past; they are still embedded in the present linguistic landscape of Aymara. Their influence persists because they provided the first systematic framework for describing the language, because their orthographic and analytical choices shaped later reconstructions, and because later scholars continue to treat them as foundational even while critically revising them [N1-R1][N1-F2][N5-F4][N5-R4][N1-R5].

Early missionary Aymara grammars preserved a core set of grammatical features, but they also distorted others in ways that shaped later linguistic understanding. The evidence suggests that missionary grammars were primarily pedagogical tools, written to teach the language in a missionary-colonial setting, and they often emphasized structures that could be mapped onto European linguistic frameworks [N5-R4]. This is directly relevant to what was preserved: grammatical categories and morphological patterns that missionaries could represent using familiar Spanish-letter orthographies and analytical conventions. The JSTOR article on Aymara literature notes that later grammars, such as the Maryknoll Instituto de Idiomas grammar, were superior to predecessors in grammatical analysis, indicating that missionaries codified a structured and analytically organized view of Aymara rather than merely transcribing it [N1-R1]. That suggests preservation of verb morphology, clause structure, and possibly word order principles, because those are the elements that can be turned into a “grammar” in the missionary sense.

At the same time, the evidence shows clear distortion. The missionary grammar tradition was shaped by the “circulation of knowledge” and by traditional models that influenced how grammarians conceptualized language [N1-F2]. This means missionaries did not always capture Aymara accurately; they interpreted it through the lens of European linguistic assumptions. The same source notes that missionary linguistics can be approached as a wide-lensed or zoomed-in phenomenon, and that the earlier grammars were shaped by the historiographical concept of knowledge circulation [N1-F2]. That implies that features not easily fit into missionary pedagogy were either omitted, simplified, or misrepresented. For example, the comparative analysis of Aymara and Quechua missionary grammars shows that grammarians distinguished coordination and subordination, but that analysis also challenges prevailing assumptions, suggesting that some distinctions were overemphasized or reinterpreted rather than neutrally recorded [N1-R5]. In other words, missionaries preserved the most teachable and analytically tractable features, while distorting or omitting those that were harder to codify or that did not align with European grammatical categories.

Orthographic and morphological choices were especially influential. The missionary grammar evidence indicates that orthography was not neutral; it was a way of recording language and shaping later understanding [N5-F4]. The “Missionary Linguistics in New France” source explains that missionary grammars were mainly written as pedagogical tools and that their orthography could be a phonemic record, a set of symbols to record the gross acoustic characteristics of speech [N5-R2]. That principle applies broadly to missionary grammars: they used Spanish-based orthographies and morphological conventions to transcribe Aymara, which in turn shaped how later scholars reconstructed historical forms. Because missionaries were focused on teaching and communication rather than on preserving an unfiltered historical record, they often chose spellings and morphological labels that aligned with European conventions rather than with indigenous phonological or morphological reality [N5-F4]. This has a lasting effect: later linguistic descriptions of Aymara continue to inherit those choices, and the boundary between historical reconstruction and modern usage becomes blurred [N5-R1].

In sum, early missionary grammars preserved the grammatical features that could be codified into a structured teaching grammar, especially verb morphology, clause structure, and coordination/subordination patterns [N1-R1][N1-R5]. They distorted features that did not fit neatly into European linguistic models, omitted features that were difficult to analyze or teach, and imposed orthographic and morphological choices that shaped later understanding [N1-F2][N5-F4]. These distortions persist because missionary orthography and methodology remain embedded in the linguistic tradition and continue to influence how Aymara is described today.

Reconstruction of historical forms versus modern usage is a key issue. The evidence suggests that missionary grammars were used as historical sources, but they were also shaped by the “circulation of knowledge” and by traditional linguistic models, which means they are best understood as intermediate records rather than direct testimony [N1-F2]. The “Missionary Linguistics in New France” source explains that missionary grammars were pedagogical tools, and that orthography could function as a phonemic record [N5-R2]. That orthographic choice matters because it influences how scholars reconstruct historical forms: if a missionary text uses a certain spelling convention, later analysts may assume that spelling reflects historical pronunciation or morphology, even if that is anachronistic or distorted [N5-F4]. The evidence also shows that modern descriptive linguistics is methodologically aware of these limitations, as the contemporary Aymara literature survey indicates that grammatical description has evolved from missionary sources into more systematic descriptive linguistics [N1-R1]. This means that missionary materials are often used as secondary evidence, not because they are primary sources, but because they provide a historical baseline against which modern descriptions can be measured.

The impact on morpheme analysis, word order, and syntax is especially clear. Missionary grammars codified a structured view of Aymara, which allowed later scholars to break the language into morphemes, establish word order principles, and analyze syntax in terms of coordination and subordination [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The comparative analysis of Aymara and Quechua missionary grammars shows that missionaries explicitly distinguished coordination and subordination, which suggests that word order and clause structure were central to their descriptive framework [N1-R5]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that missionary grammars were influenced by traditional models and by the broader missionary circulation of linguistic knowledge, so their analysis was not always neutral [N1-F2]. That means modern morpheme analysis, word order, and syntax are often shaped by the same assumptions that missionaries brought into the grammar, even as later scholars try to refine or correct them [N5-F4]. In short, missionary sources remain authoritative not because they are infallible, but because they established the vocabulary and analytical categories that later descriptive linguistics inherited and adapted.

The missionary grammar legacy continues to affect regional and dialectal descriptions of Aymara in at least three ways: dialects influenced by colonial sources differ from each other, regional borrowing aligns with missionary orthography, and current descriptions often treat historical sources as authoritative. The evidence on regional variation shows that Aymara is spoken across a wide area, including the southern highlands, northern highlands, and northern regions, with different varieties and dialects [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The “Expansions and language shift in prehistory” sources add that in many parts of the southern highlands, Quechua came to replace Aymara varieties spoken there earlier, and that Inka expansion spread Aymara into the Altiplano of Bolivia and out of the southern highlands [N4-R3][N4-R4]. This historical contact and language shift imply that dialectal differences in Aymara are not only natural variation but also shaped by colonial and postcolonial contact with Spanish, Quechua, and other languages [N4-R2][N4-R5]. That makes dialectal descriptions difficult because the same grammatical features may appear differently across regions, partly because each region has been influenced by different colonial sources.

Regional borrowing and alignment with missionary orthography are also evident. The evidence shows that missionary grammars were written in Spanish and that their orthography was often a phonemic record, a set of symbols to record the gross acoustic characteristics of speech [N5-R2]. That orthography was not neutral; it shaped how Aymara was represented and taught, which in turn influenced regional borrowing and alignment. The “missionary linguistics” source explains that missionary grammars were pedagogical tools, so their orthography and morphological choices were designed to support teaching rather than to preserve an unfiltered historical record [N5-R4]. As a result, dialects that were exposed to missionary education or missionary orthography may have retained or adopted spelling conventions that align with those sources, even as they continue to evolve. The evidence also suggests that modern Aymara usage is affected by broader contact with Spanish and Andean languages, which means regional dialects can reflect both indigenous variation and colonial influence [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Current descriptions that treat historical sources as authoritative are another important effect. The JSTOR article on Aymara literature notes that later grammars, such as the Maryknoll Instituto de Idiomas grammar, were superior to predecessors in grammatical analysis, which implies that historical missionary sources are often seen as foundational even if they are not the most accurate or comprehensive [N1-R1]. The comparative analysis of missionary grammars also shows that missionaries distinguished coordination and subordination, and that this analysis challenges prevailing assumptions, which suggests that modern scholars do not simply discard missionary texts but instead reinterpret them as historical sources [N1-R5]. The same source also discusses missionary linguistics as a wide-lensed phenomenon shaped by the circulation of knowledge, reinforcing the idea that missionary sources are treated as authoritative because they were among the first systematic descriptions of Aymara [N1-F2]. In practice, this means that dialectal descriptions may rely on missionary orthography, colonial-era structures, and early grammatical categories even when those sources are imperfect or biased [N5-F4]. The result is that regional and dialectal descriptions of Aymara are shaped by both internal variation and external colonial influence, with missionary sources continuing to be a key point of reference.

Early missionary Aymara grammars preserved a core set of grammatical features, but they also distorted others in ways that shaped later linguistic understanding. The evidence suggests that missionary grammars were primarily pedagogical tools, written to teach the language in a missionary-colonial setting, and they often emphasized structures that could be mapped onto European linguistic frameworks [N5-R4]. This is directly relevant to what was preserved: grammatical categories and morphological patterns that missionaries could represent using familiar Spanish-letter orthographies and analytical conventions. The JSTOR article on Aymara literature notes that later grammars, such as the Maryknoll Instituto de Idiomas grammar, were superior to predecessors in grammatical analysis, indicating that missionaries codified a structured and analytically organized view of Aymara rather than merely transcribing it [N1-R1]. That suggests preservation of verb morphology, clause structure, and possibly word order principles, because those are the elements that can be turned into a “grammar” in the missionary sense.

At the same time, the evidence shows clear distortion. The missionary grammar tradition was shaped by the “circulation of knowledge” and by traditional models that influenced how grammarians conceptualized language [N1-F2]. This means missionaries did not always capture Aymara accurately; they interpreted it through the lens of European linguistic assumptions. The same source notes that missionary linguistics can be approached as a wide-lensed or zoomed-in phenomenon, and that the earlier grammars were shaped by the historiographical concept of knowledge circulation [N1-F2]. That implies that features not easily fit into missionary pedagogy were either omitted, simplified, or misrepresented. For example, the comparative analysis of Aymara and Quechua missionary grammars shows that grammarians distinguished coordination and subordination, but that analysis also challenges prevailing assumptions, suggesting that some distinctions were overemphasized or reinterpreted rather than neutrally recorded [N1-R5]. In other words, missionaries preserved the most teachable and analytically tractable features, while distorting or omitting those that were harder to codify or that did not align with European grammatical categories.

Orthographic and morphological choices were especially influential. The missionary grammar evidence indicates that orthography was not neutral; it was a way of recording language and shaping later understanding [N5-F4]. The “Missionary Linguistics in New France” source explains that missionary grammars were mainly written as pedagogical tools and that their orthography could be a phonemic record, a set of symbols to record the gross acoustic characteristics of speech [N5-R2]. That principle applies broadly to missionary grammars: they used Spanish-based orthographies and morphological conventions to transcribe Aymara, which in turn shaped how later scholars reconstructed historical forms. Because missionaries were focused on teaching and communication rather than on preserving an unfiltered historical record, they often chose spellings and morphological labels that aligned with European conventions rather than with indigenous phonological or morphological reality [N5-F4]. This has a lasting effect: later linguistic descriptions of Aymara continue to inherit those choices, and the boundary between historical reconstruction and modern usage becomes blurred [N5-R1].

In sum, early missionary grammars preserved the grammatical features that could be codified into a structured teaching grammar, especially verb morphology, clause structure, and coordination/subordination patterns [N1-R1][N1-R5]. They distorted features that did not fit neatly into European linguistic models, omitted features that were difficult to analyze or teach, and imposed orthographic and morphological choices that shaped later understanding [N1-F2][N5-F4]. These distortions persist because missionary orthography and methodology remain embedded in the linguistic tradition and continue to influence how Aymara is described today.

The orthographic evidence also reveals bias: missionary orthography was a phonemic record, but it was still a mediated representation of speech, not an unfiltered transcription [N5-R2]. Later adaptation is evident in the fact that contemporary descriptive linguistics has moved beyond missionary sources, yet those sources remain foundational because they provided the initial analytical categories [N5-F4].

In short, comparative missionary analysis shows that Aymara and Quechua were not treated as isolated languages but as part of a broader Andean linguistic tradition, and that missionary grammars reveal both the shared assumptions of the time and the biases that later scholars have had to correct or refine [N1-R5][N1-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-F4].

---

## 5) Overall conclusion

The continued influence of early Aymara grammars is therefore multidimensional. They preserved a core grammatical structure that later scholars built upon, but they also distorted or omitted other features. They shaped modern linguistic analysis and description by establishing secondary-evidence status, reconstruction norms, and analytic categories. They affected regional and dialectal descriptions by embedding colonial orthography and colonial-era assumptions into dialectal work. And they revealed broader linguistic patterns through comparative analysis with Quechua and other Andean languages, exposing both shared assumptions and missionary bias.

Taken together, these sources show that early missionary grammars do not simply belong to the past; they are still embedded in the present linguistic landscape of Aymara. Their influence persists because they provided the first systematic framework for describing the language, because their orthographic and analytical choices shaped later reconstructions, and because later scholars continue to treat them as foundational even while critically revising them [N1-R1][N1-F2][N5-F4][N5-R4][N1-R5].
